answer_text:
To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is - that was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. We confess him as the Scriptures give him: God's own Son, born of Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised on the third day, ascended and seated at the Father's right hand. We hold the ancient creeds without revision. Where our teaching becomes distinctly ours is not in who Jesus is, but in what God has done in him and how we receive what he gives.

What is ours to speak plainly is this: God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved in Christ - not anything foreseen or earned. That election we hold as a settled ground, not a threat. And we will not send you searching your own heart for proof of it. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and it rejected looking for that apart from him. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. So we turned it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

At the Supper, Christ himself is what is truly given. Not his body confined to bread we can chew and store away. Not a sacrifice repeated. But Christ himself, received by the Spirit, by whoever takes him believing.

What we actually have of Christ is not a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Our own founder said so of himself, and we made it our own rule: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better — but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

The text reached us the way it reached every church of the Latin West: copied, translated, carried forward through the generations that came before us. We did not claim a purer line back to the apostles than Rome possessed. We claimed that what Rome had added to that text — the repeated sacrifice, the images, the binding force of its own accumulated tradition — Scripture itself does not warrant. So we let those additions go, and held to what the text itself says.

The same Hebrew and Greek manuscripts Rome read, we read. The difference was not in the source. It was in what we allowed to bind us when we read it.

We have no method for making yourself believe, and we will not give you one. What we would ask is whether you have been pressing yourself to produce faith by your own effort, searching inward to see whether you believe hard enough. That is the wrong direction entirely. Faith is not something you generate by examining yourself more carefully. It comes from looking outward, toward what has been promised.

Our confession says it plainly: Christ is the mirror in which election is seen. The question is not whether you can manage to manufacture certainty about him inside your own mind. The question is whether you have heard the promise held out, and whether you can look at it. We did not tell anyone to test their own heart for proof that they believe strongly enough. We told them to look at Christ himself, held out in Scripture.

What we have of Christ is not a chain of living witnesses stretching back to him. Fifteen hundred years stand between his life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold it sufficient. So the answer is not that you need to feel something more intensely than you do. The answer is that the promise is written down, and it can be looked at. Bullinger wrote: “We reject those who try to find out, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen. ... Let ... Christ be the mirror in which we look at our predestination.”

We cannot tell you that this will immediately quiet every troubled mind. What we can tell you is that a mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. So we turned it outward instead.

We hold what the church has always held. Jesus is fully God, one with the Father and the Spirit - three persons, one divine essence. That was never our quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. We did not invent a new teaching about Christ's own nature. We received it from the whole church's own confession, and we held it.

What is distinctly ours is not who Christ is, but what we were taught about who is chosen in him. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned. We hold that as a settled ground, not a threat. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and rejected looking for that apart from him.

This conviction about God's choosing runs deep in the church's own memory. Our pastor at Geneva drew it directly from Augustine's own anti-Pelagian writings - total depravity, unconditional election, irresistible grace. Calvin named Augustine his primary authority next to Scripture itself. It is a theological line across eleven centuries, not something we invented.

We also hold that God's providence is his own continuous, active care over everything he made. He is not a distant first cause who set the world going and stepped back. He keeps caring for it.

God is one, and he is sovereign. That is where we began, and where we returned most often. He made all things, he rules all things, and nothing happens outside his will. This is not a claim we reached for to settle an argument. It is what Scripture itself shows us, and so we held it.

He chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. Not because of anything he saw coming in the one chosen - not their faith, not their works, not even their foreseen willingness to believe. The choosing came first, and it came from him alone. Both Zurich and Geneva held this. Geneva built it into a full system. Zurich stated it more briefly, as pastoral comfort.

We did not hold this as a threat. We held it as the ground of a settled life. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. So we turned it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given.

He is holy, and he is just. He will not overlook sin. But he is also merciful, and his mercy is not earned. Christ's one sacrifice answered the justice. The Spirit gives Christ to whoever receives him believing.

We held one conviction, tested two ways. Scripture alone may bind a church; what it does not warrant, no one may require of us. Where we disagreed, the conviction itself pointed to the method: test the claim against Scripture, in public, with witnesses who could answer back. At Zurich, that conviction was enacted through Disputation. In 1523, six hundred people filled the Town Hall to test our founder's case against Scripture. The council ruled for it and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. The council itself, not a bishop and not a synod elsewhere, said what the text had yielded. At Geneva, the same conviction was enacted differently. Doctrine was built up article by article and taught to the whole population through the Catechism. When our own predestination doctrine was publicly challenged at Geneva in 1551, it was that body and those pastors who answered the challenge.

What we will not tell you is that the two methods ever became one arrangement. At Zurich, the council governed church and city together from our first days. At Geneva, the Consistory fought for its independence from that kind of magistrate's claim, and only by 1555 substantially won it. We hold that unresolved.

The evidence for how it worked is the confession and argument that survive. We have the text of what was tested and what was ruled. What we do not have is an ordinary believer's own account of a Sunday service, or of a Consistory summons, or of what any of this felt like to live through. That silence is not a flaw in what we hold; it is what the record actually gives us.

We made more room for that struggle than you might think, though not in the way a modern soul might expect. What we refused to do was send someone deeper into themselves to search for proof they were chosen. Our confession named that kind of searching directly and rejected it - not as weakness, but as the wrong mirror entirely. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it.

So we turned the question outward instead. Christ himself, held out plainly in the promise, is where we said election is rightly seen. Not your own certainty about it, tested again and again until the testing itself becomes the torment. The promise was not written to be verified by how settled you feel. It was written to be looked at.

That is a different question, and a harder one. At Geneva, our Consistory - pastors and lay elders together - held the whole population's ordinary conduct answerable to what we professed. Its harshest step was excommunication: shut out of the Supper and the visible church until genuine repentance was shown. What we cannot give you is a single real case - a named person, a real hearing, what was said, what happened to them afterward. That record exists, in Geneva's consistory registers. It has not reached us.

We held that every person born into this world, from the moment of birth, carries the full weight of Adam's own fall. That guilt is not something earned by our own later choosing - it is inherited, passed down through the whole human line from the first disobedience. We did not teach this as a cruelty. We taught it as the settled ground from which God's own free election becomes clear: no one is saved because they deserved it, and no one is lost because they failed to measure up. The choosing was God's alone, made before the world began, and nothing foreseen or earned in any of us decided it.

What we will not do is send you searching your own heart for proof that the guilt has been lifted. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and it refused looking for that apart from him. The guilt is real. The choosing is sure. The place to look is outward, toward Christ held out in the promise, not inward toward a conscience that will only find more of itself the longer it searches.

We read Scripture as the one sufficient rule for both what we teach and how we govern ourselves. What it warrants stands; what it does not warrant may not be required of anyone. That conviction shaped everything we did, though we tested it two different ways.

At Zurich, our founder set aside the old fixed calendar of readings and began preaching straight through Matthew. When that provoked a crisis, we held a public disputation: six hundred priests and laymen gathered in the Town Hall in 1523, and our founder's case was tested aloud, article by article, before the whole assembly. The council itself judged what the text had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. That was how Zurich chose to reform - by argument in the open, tested until the council said the matter was settled.

Geneva built the same conviction differently. There it was worked out book by book, doctrine raised article by article, until the whole shape of what Scripture teaches stood complete. It was taught to everyone through the Catechism and tested against ordinary conduct by the Consistory. Where Zurich disputed, Geneva constructed - but both cities held that Scripture alone was enough to settle the question, and that no church tradition or council decree could add to it or stand against it.

We never claimed Scripture was easy, or that every reader would arrive at the same place unaided. What we claimed was that where we had not rightly understood it, we would be taught better - but only from Scripture itself, not from a chain of memory we did not possess and did not need.
